A Cochrane review on massage, with or without aromatherapy, in people with cancer rated most outcomes as very low certainty; only one outcome (medium-term anxiety, aromatherapy with massage) was rated moderate. Massage can be a support for relaxation, not a treatment for the disease, and should be discussed with the oncology team.

A 2015 Cochrane review (25 studies, 3,096 participants) rated the evidence as low or very low quality. Massage reduced pain in the short term compared with no treatment, but not in the long term, and the authors said they have “very little confidence” that massage is effective. No serious adverse events were reported; most often, pain increased temporarily.

A conference abstract (World Physiotherapy) on the update of a Cochrane review (44 studies) concluded that the studies are of low quality and that no firm recommendation can be made for or against massage. Small to medium effects appeared mainly after large, repeated doses of massage; the reported side effects were minor and transient, such as local tenderness.
